prerequisites: basic knowledge of mathematical analysis: complex numbers, derivatives and integrals, and linear differential equations
basic knowledge of linear algebra: vectors, matrices, determinants, eigenvalues and systems of linear equations
basic knowledge of physics and electrical circuit analysis

learning_outcomes.text: describe the main mathematical representations of continuous-time dynamical systems
explain the dynamic behaviour, stability and performance of linear time-invariant systems
explain the operation of feedback control systems and the main criteria for the design of basic automatic control systems

derive state-space and input
output models of simple physical systems and analyse their response
apply the Laplace transform and time- and frequency-domain methods to LTI systems

assess stability and performance using the Routh
Hurwitz criterion and Bode plots
simulate dynamical and control systems in MATLAB/Simulink and compare analytical and numerical results
design basic PID controllers and compensator networks subject to steady-state and dynamic specifications
consult and use textbooks, lecture notes, manuals and technical documentation, and plan, complete and clearly document an analysis or design procedure
select the analysis or design method most appropriate to the assigned problem
critically interpret results, check their consistency, and discuss the assumptions and limitations of the adopted solution
present analysis and design solutions in written and oral form, using appropriate technical terminology
independently organise individual work and effectively discuss exercises and case studies in written and oral form
independently use learning resources and software documentation to consolidate or further explore course topics
relate the acquired knowledge to advanced courses in control, automation and robotics

syllabus_topics: Modelling and simulation
Time- and frequency-domain analysis of continuous-time LTI systems

Routh
Hurwitz stability analysis
Bode plots
Feedback systems
Design of PID controllers and lead/lag compensators

State-space and input
output representations
Lumped-parameter linear models of simple electrical, mechanical, hydraulic and thermal systems
Numerical simulation of dynamical systems using MATLAB and Simulink
Review of the Laplace transform and inverse transform
Transfer function and impulse response
Free and forced response

Stability and the Routh
Hurwitz criterion
Step response and time-domain performance indices
Harmonic analysis and frequency response
Bode plots
Structure and properties of feedback systems
Internal stability
Stability margins
Steady-state specifications: steady-state error and system type
Time-domain dynamic specifications: overshoot, settling time and rise time
Frequency-domain dynamic specifications: resonance peak, bandwidth, phase margin and crossover frequency
Approximate relationships between time- and frequency-domain specifications
Basic compensator networks: lag and lead compensators
Trial-and-error design in the frequency domain
PID controllers and basic tuning criteria
teaching_methods: guided use of textbooks, manuals and technical documentation
supporting materials and activities on Moodle

assessment_methods.method: Written test - Theoretical knowledge and conceptual understanding (multiple-choice questions or exemption test)
Written test - Analysis skills (exercise on LTI feedback system)
Written test - Design and problem-solving skills (design of feedback control system)
Oral examination (compulsory discussion of written test exercises)
Optional full oral examination (at student's request)

assessment_rules: Learning is assessed through a compulsory written test and an oral examination. The written test has a maximum raw score of 31 points, capped at 30/30 for assessment purposes. The oral examination includes a compulsory discussion of the exercises from the written test. An optional full oral examination may be taken if the written test mark is at least 14/30, which can change the written-test mark by -5/30 to +5/30. The final mark is the written-test mark after the compulsory discussion, potentially adjusted by the optional full oral examination, and is capped at 30/30; a result below 18/30 is a fail.
